title: Postal, telecom and government employees
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Postal, telecom and government employees: what the federations cover, how the NPS and the Unified Pension Scheme differ, and what unites services that face the citizen.
body:
Some of the people who keep the state running are rarely thought of as workers at all. A postman climbing a village lane, a telecom technician restoring a line after a storm, a clerk in a Collectorate and a block-level employee of a State government are all part of the public workforce, and all are covered by service rules that are very different from those of a factory. BMS has long been active among such employees. The federations on its website include the **Bharatiya Postal Employees Federation**, the **Indian Telecom Employees Federation**, the **Kendriya Karamchari Mahasangh** for central government employees, the **Rashtriya Rajya Karamchari Mahasangh** for State government employees and the **Sarkari Karmchari Rashtriya Parisangh**. This post takes the three groups in turn and looks at what they have in common.

## The postal worker

The post office is the oldest public service that reaches almost every village. According to Wikipedia, India Post had 164,999 post offices as of March 2025, of which 149,385 were in rural areas, about 90 per cent of the total. Its workforce was recorded at 4,57,997 in 2024. The India Post Payments Bank, inaugurated on 1 September 2018, is run as a department of India Post and uses the post office network to bring banking to people far from a bank branch.

That reach is built by two kinds of employees. Departmental staff are regular government employees. **Gramin Dak Sevaks**, who run many of the rural branch post offices and deliver mail, have traditionally been engaged on different terms, and their service conditions differ from those of departmental employees. Unions have long argued that people who do a government service every day, and are the face of the Department in rural India, deserve conditions that match the importance of the work. Questions that arise in discussions include the status of Gramin Dak Sevaks, their allowances, how workload is measured when a post office also handles banking and insurance, and the hours that the job really takes.

The postal worker also illustrates how the nature of the job has changed. The delivery of letters is now only part of the work; parcels, payments, savings and insurance have moved to the centre. Unions point out that targets for sales and transactions can fall on people who were recruited to deliver mail.

## Telecom

BSNL was established by the Government on 1 October 2000. In the years since, following the corporatisation of BSNL and MTNL, the questions for employees have been the revival of the companies, the position of employees and pensioners and the retention of a public sector presence in telecom.

Wikipedia records some of the milestones. A revival package for BSNL and MTNL was announced on 24 October 2019, covering asset monetisation, fund raising, spectrum and a voluntary retirement scheme. A second package, worth Rs 1.64 lakh crore, was approved on 27 July 2022, and merged the broadband company BBNL into BSNL. The same article says that BSNL has since installed more than 40,000 4G-enabled towers, and that on 27 September 2025 the Prime Minister launched its indigenously developed 4G network and commissioned 97,500 towers.

For employees, these developments are not abstract. A voluntary retirement scheme changes the age profile of a workforce and the load on those who stay. Revival depends on whether the company can deliver reliable services in rural and remote areas and that in turn depends on investment, on staffing and on the morale of the people in the field. BMS's general position is that a public sector presence in telecom matters and that the workforce should be a partner in its revival.

## Government employees

The central and State government employees' federations deal with the largest and most diverse group. Their concerns have included the pension system, the pay commission, dearness allowance and the regularisation of contract staff.

**Pension.** For central government employees recruited on or after 1 January 2004, the New Pension System replaced the old defined-benefit pension. The Ministry of Finance notification that mandated it was issued on 22 December 2003. In place of a fixed pension, the new system gives an outcome that depends on contributions and investment returns. This has been the heart of the demand for a return to the old pension scheme.

The Unified Pension Scheme was approved by the Union Cabinet on **24 August 2024**, to take effect from 1 April 2025. According to the official account carried by AIR, it promises an assured pension of 50 per cent of the average basic pay of the last twelve months before retirement, for a minimum qualifying service of 25 years, with proportionate payments for service of less than that down to ten years. It guarantees a minimum pension of Rs 10,000 a month after at least ten years of service and a family pension of 60 per cent of the employee's pension. It is expected to benefit about 23 lakh central government employees.

To see what that means, consider an illustration, which is only an example and not a real case: if an employee's average basic pay over the last year was Rs 60,000, a person with 25 years of service would be assured a pension of Rs 30,000 a month under the formula. The point of the example is that the formula is assured, unlike a market-linked fund. Employees' federations took part in the consultations, and some of them have said that the scheme still does not give what the old pension did, which is why the issue continues in discussions.

**Pay commission.** The wage structure of government employees is reviewed by pay commissions, and the arrival of a new commission is a major occasion for unions, which prepare detailed memoranda on pay, allowances and the treatment of different categories.

**Regularisation of contract staff.** A growing share of government work is done by people who are not regular employees. The BMS Kendriya Karya Samithi, meeting in Bhopal on 22 to 24 August 2025, welcomed a Haryana Government decision to regularise contract workers under its Kaushal Vikas Yojana. It is an example of an area in which State-level decisions matter.

## What unites the three

These are people who serve the citizen directly. A pensioner collecting a pension, a farmer waiting for a money order, a family waiting for a telephone line and a student waiting for a certificate all depend on someone in these services. BMS argues that a government that treats its own employees with respect is better able to serve the people, and that stability in service conditions is a precondition for good service.

The common agenda, then, includes a pension that offers real security after retirement, fair treatment of those on contract or in special categories such as Gramin Dak Sevaks, staffing that matches the workload and a voice for employees when decisions are made about the restructuring of their departments. None of this requires opposing the Government for its own sake. It requires that those who do the work are asked before changes are made.
